The Black-winged kite (Elanus caeruleus) exhibits a highly distinctive pattern of post-natal development that is closely tied to thermal conditions during the incubation period. Eggs maintained at an average temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] complete their incubation phase and hatch after approximately 26 days [ab = approximately 26 days], although field records indicate that successful hatching can occur anywhere from 27 to 31 days depending on microclimatic variation at the nest site. Upon hatching, the newly emerged nestlings register a wet weight at birth of 18.6 grams [Wwb = 18.6 grams], a remarkably low mass given the species' eventual adult size, and one that underscores the altricial nature of the chicks at this earliest stage. The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg, measured immediately after oviposition, is 21 grams [Ww0 = 21 grams], indicating that the egg itself constitutes a substantial maternal investment relative to the neonatal mass. This pattern is consistent with that seen in many small to medium-sized raptors, where a large egg provides the developing embryo with sufficient yolk reserves to sustain growth until pipping.

During the nestling phase, growth proceeds at a rapid pace as the developing chick transitions from dependence on yolk reserves to dependence on parental provisioning. Under typical ambient conditions recorded during the active season, which often approach 40 °C [T = 40 °C] in the species' subtropical and savanna habitats, the fledging stage is reached at approximately 32.5 days after hatching [tx = approximately 32.5 days after hatching], with a documented range of 32 to 35 days reported across various populations. This relatively short nestling period is typical of elanine kites and is thought to be an adaptation that reduces the risk of nest predation. The achievement of fledging marks the point at which the young bird can sustain powered flight, although parental provisioning may continue for several weeks thereafter. The developmental timing observed in this species appears to be finely tuned to the thermal environment, as elevated brooding temperatures accelerate feather growth and muscle maturation, allowing for an earlier departure from the nest.

Sexual maturation in the Black-winged kite follows a substantially longer timeline than the fledging period, reflecting the prolonged period of somatic growth and foraging skill acquisition required before individuals can engage in reproductive activities. Under the thermal conditions typical of the species' active season, which commonly reach 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the time since birth at puberty has been estimated at 97.5 days after hatching [tp = 97.5 days after hatching], although some field observations suggest that gonadal development may be completed as early as 32 to 35 days after hatching in individuals raised under particularly favorable conditions. This broad range likely reflects intraspecific variation in food availability and territory quality, with well-provisioned individuals reaching sexual maturity considerably earlier than those in suboptimal habitats. The attainment of puberty is a critical milestone, as it marks the onset of gametogenesis and the capacity to produce viable gametes, although actual breeding is often deferred.

The onset of first reproduction in the Black-winged kite occurs approximately one year after the individual's own hatching, a delay that is common among raptors that require extensive practice in hunting and territory establishment before attempting to breed. Field studies conducted under ambient temperatures near 40 °C [T = 40 °C] indicate that the time since birth at first brood is 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], meaning that most individuals do not breed until their second calendar year. This deferred first breeding is thought to be a consequence of the need to acquire a high-quality territory and to perfect the aerial hunting techniques necessary for capturing small mammals and reptiles. Females typically produce a single clutch containing 3.5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3.5 eggs per clutch] and initiate only one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year], resulting in a relatively low annual reproductive output of 3.5 eggs per year [Ri = 3.5 eggs per year] compared to many other birds of comparable body size.

Adult body mass in the Black-winged kite shows pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females attaining a substantially larger ultimate wet weight than males. The ultimate wet weight for adult females reaches 258.5 grams [Wwi = 258.5 grams], whereas the ultimate wet weight for male individuals is considerably smaller at 237 grams [Wwi = 237 grams]. This size difference is typical of many raptor species, in which the larger female is better able to defend the nest and incubate eggs effectively, while the smaller, more agile male specializes in hunting and provisioning. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species under natural conditions, when measured at an average ambient temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], is 6 years [am = 6 years], a longevity that is modest among raptors but consistent with the high mortality rates experienced by small-bodied, open-country birds. Comparative data from related species in the genus Elanus suggest that the Black-winged kite's life history, characterized by a single small clutch per year and a relatively short lifespan, represents an adaptive response to the unpredictable prey base of its grassland and savanna habitats.
